title: eMudhra intermediate CA compromise
summary: Private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authorities were compromised: six of them issue TLS certificates and two sign code. Anyone holding one of the six TLS keys could issue a certificate for any website. Those six hold 12 certificates between them, two each: one issued by AAA Certificate Services, one by emSign Root TLS CA - G3. A client is exposed where it still trusts the roots those intermediates chain to and does not itself block the intermediates; a fixed Node, Go, Electron or Deno, and Apple's own trust evaluation, block them whatever trust list they read.
canarySource: The 12 test hosts are the advisory's own (emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/#check). Each serves a certificate chained to one compromised intermediate.

distrustedRoots.name: AAA Certificate Services (Comodo, via the Sectigo cross-sign)

withdrawnKeys.name: emSign Root TLS CA - G3
withdrawnKeys.why: The CA that issued six of the 12 compromised intermediates. Its own key is not among the eight compromised ones, but a bundle holding either of its two certificates vouches for all six: curl, git and the built-in perl take every CA certificate in a --cacert file as a trust anchor, and the self-signed copy is a full anchor for every reader. Both certificates carry this one key, so matching by key covers both.

withdrawnKeysNote: Seven keys that a bundle must not hold, over and above the two withdrawn roots in distrustedRoots. Six of them are the compromised TLS intermediate keys: six keys in 12 certificates, because each intermediate was issued twice, once under emSign Root TLS CA - G3 and once under AAA Certificate Services (Sectigo's cross-sign). The seventh is emSign Root TLS CA - G3's own key. These are keys, not trust anchors any root programme listed, so they are not in distrustedRoots: that array drives the probe's forced-roots control and has one PEM file and one canary group per entry. spkiSha256 is the SHA-256 of the SubjectPublicKeyInfo as it ships; ecX is the X coordinate of the EC point (48 bytes, lowercase hex), which every encoding of the point carries and which is what fix/fix-macos.sh compares. Each value was derived from the certificate twice, with LibreSSL 3.3.6 and with OpenSSL 4.0.3, and refused if it came out as the SHA-256 of no input (e3b0c442...).

fixes.curl:/usr/bin/curl:darwin: macOS's built-in curl, git, python3 and openssl read /etc/ssl/cert.pem. Apple says macOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3 and 15.8.3, released on 9 Nov 2026, remove the withdrawn roots from that file (support.apple.com/en-us/149555), so update macOS (System Settings, General, Software Update). If you can't update, download Wardlatch's Mac fix in Safari (www.deimoscore.com/wardlatch/#mac), which checks its own work and keeps a backup. Or the advisory's fix (backs the file up first, asks for your Mac password): sudo cp /etc/ssl/cert.pem /etc/ssl/cert.pem.bak && sudo awk '/^(###|===) /{skip=0} /^=== .*\/CN=(AAA Certificate Services|emSign ECC Root CA - G3)$/{skip=1} !skip' /etc/ssl/cert.pem.bak | sudo tee /etc/ssl/cert.pem > /dev/null
fixes.curl:/usr/bin/curl:darwin:fixed: Apple's update should have removed the withdrawn roots from /etc/ssl/cert.pem, but the built-in curl still accepted the test hosts. This Mac runs macOS {macos}, and Apple says 27.2.1, 26.7.3, 15.8.3 and later remove those roots from that file (support.apple.com/en-us/149555). Check the file: openssl crl2pkcs7 -nocrl -certfile /etc/ssl/cert.pem | openssl pkcs7 -print_certs -noout | grep -E 'emSign ECC Root CA - G3|AAA Certificate Services' lists either root still in it. If it lists one, the update did not replace the file (we measured one Mac on 10 Nov 2026 whose update from 27.2 to 27.2.1 replaced a hand-changed file with Apple's; other Macs and releases weren't measured) or an older copy was put back after it; Apple says not to restore a backup made before the update. To remove them, download Wardlatch's Mac fix in Safari (www.deimoscore.com/wardlatch/#mac), which checks its own work and keeps a backup. Or the advisory's fix (backs the file up first, asks for your Mac password): sudo cp /etc/ssl/cert.pem /etc/ssl/cert.pem.bak && sudo awk '/^(###|===) /{skip=0} /^=== .*\/CN=(AAA Certificate Services|emSign ECC Root CA - G3)$/{skip=1} !skip' /etc/ssl/cert.pem.bak | sudo tee /etc/ssl/cert.pem > /dev/null. If it lists neither, please report this: https://github.com/deimos-hq/wardlatch/issues

fixes.curl:linux: Update your distribution's ca-certificates package (Debian 12: 20250419~deb12u2, Debian 13: 20250419+deb13u1). Until it ships, see the advisory's Linux workaround.
fixes.python:linux: Update your distribution's ca-certificates package; Python's default context reads the system store.
fixes.curl: Update the CA bundle this curl uses (Homebrew: brew upgrade ca-certificates, fixed in 2026-09-25_1 and later).
fixes.node: Update Node.js to 26.12.1, 24.22.1 or 22.23.4 (released 21 Oct 2026; nodejs/node#66871 and the NSS 3.131.1 roots) from nodejs.org or your version manager, then rebuild anything that bundles Node. On an older line: run it with --use-openssl-ca and SSL_CERT_FILE pointing at an updated bundle (for example the cleaned /etc/ssl/cert.pem).
fixes.python-certifi: Upgrade certifi in this environment to 2026.10.19 or newer: pip install -U certifi (uv: uv lock --upgrade-package certifi).
fixes.requests-ca-bundle: REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE points requests and pip at a bundle that still trusts the distrusted roots. Remove the AAA Certificate Services and emSign ECC Root CA - G3 certificates from that file, or point REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE at an updated bundle (certifi 2026.10.19 or newer, or your distribution's updated store).
fixes.python: Upgrade the CA bundle this Python uses. python.org builds: pip install -U certifi (2026.10.19+) or run 'Install Certificates.command'.
fixes.macos-system: Apple blocks the compromised certificates for Safari and its own apps, which use Apple's trust layer rather than a file. That block arrives automatically as certificate configuration data, not in a software update, so there is nothing to install for this layer. Keep the system updated for everything else. For /etc/ssl/cert.pem, the file the built-in command-line tools read, Apple says macOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3 and 15.8.3 (9 Nov 2026) remove the withdrawn roots (support.apple.com/en-us/149555): see the curl line. On a Mac that can't update to one of them, an update can put Apple's original file back (updates to 26.7.2 on 27 Oct and 27.2 on 28 Oct did, as we measured): run the test after each software update. We haven't measured what an update to 27.2.1, 26.7.3 or 15.8.3 does to a file already changed by hand.
fixes.container: This container's image has the old trust list. Rebuild it on a fixed base (docker build --pull --no-cache), or pull the maintainer's fixed image (docker compose pull && docker compose up -d). For an image nobody maintains, mount the host's fixed bundle read-only: www.deimoscore.com/wardlatch/#homelab

appleFix.said: Starting in macOS 27.2.1, macOS also blocks these 12 certificates in the command-line tools included with macOS or the Xcode Command Line Tools. It also removes the two root CA certificates that the 12 certificates chain to from /etc/ssl/cert.pem, along with three other eMudhra root CA certificates. macOS 26.7.3 and macOS 15.8.3 also include this protection.

notCovered: A compiled program does not pick this change up from the system, so it has to be rebuilt or replaced: rebuild Go programs with Go 1.27.3 or 1.26.10 (on Linux and in containers: on a Mac, Go programs use Apple's own certificate check, and one Go 1.26.2 program on macOS 27.2.1 was measured refusing the 12 certificates, whatever SSL_CERT_FILE said); update Electron apps to 44.9.1, 43.8.1 or 42.11.16; Rust: rustls-webpki 0.103.16, webpki-roots 1.0.10. Browsers: Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari block the intermediates through their own updates; check yours at the advisory's #check page.

binaries.fix: Update cloudflared to 2026.10.2 or later (Homebrew: brew upgrade cloudflared). It carries its own trust list, per Cloudflare's advisory.

Upgrade Go to 1.27.3 or 1.26.10, then rebuild and redeploy every program built with it. A Go program reads its trust list at run time, from the operating system's store (and on macOS through Apple's verifier), rather than carrying one from the toolchain. What the toolchain does compile in is the refusal of these intermediates, which is why a rebuild is needed: Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 add that refusal in crypto/x509, and a program built by an older Go keeps accepting them however up to date the system store is.
